scenes.visual: fed vs fasted, three precursor streams
scenes.narration: Think of your body as running two completely different supply chains depending on whether you have just eaten. In the fed state, blood glucose is abundant, so cells simply burn it. Glycolysis feeds the Krebs cycle, which makes ATP. But hours after a meal, glucose runs scarce, and the brain and red blood cells still demand it constantly. Now the body switches to gluconeogenesis, manufacturing glucose from non-sugar raw materials. Three streams feed that factory. Lactate from muscle and red cells, alanine and glutamine from muscle, and glycerol from fat breakdown. Hold onto this fed versus fasted framing because it explains every regulatory decision we make today.

scenes.narration: Most of glycolysis is freely reversible, and gluconeogenesis simply runs those steps backward. The problem lives in exactly three places where glycolysis releases so much free energy that the reaction is effectively one-way. Look at the numbers—hexokinase, phosphofructokinase, and pyruvate kinase—each have large negative ΔG values, so reversing them directly is impossible. Gluconeogenesis solves this with four dedicated bypass enzymes, shown in orange, glucose-6-phosphatase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, and the pyruvate carboxylase, plus PEP carboxykinase pair. Notice that pyruvate to PEP is split into two reactions, whose combined energetics make the climb feasible. Same map, different roads around the cliffs.

scenes.narration: Here is a logistics problem the cell must solve. Pyruvate carboxylase lives inside the mitochondrial matrix, so oxaloacetate is made there. But the next enzyme, PEP carboxykinase, works in the cytoplasm in this route, and the membrane has no oxaloacetate transporter. The workaround is elegant. Reduce oxaloacetate to malate, which can cross, then reoxidize malate back to oxaloacetate on the other side. From pyruvate or alanine, that second oxidation also regenerates cytoplasmic NADH, which gluconeogenesis needs later. So one shuttle accomplishes two jobs at once, moving carbon out and delivering reducing power exactly where the downstream reactions will consume it.

scenes.narration: Why does gluconeogenesis need its own enzymes instead of just reversing glycolysis? Think of it as a bargain the cell strikes with thermodynamics. Glycolysis releases energy, about 85 kilojoules per mole, so it is downhill and spontaneous. Gluconeogenesis consumes energy, and that extra cost, the six nucleotide triphosphate equivalents, is precisely what tips the synthetic direction to also be favorable. That means both pathways could run at once in the same cell, a futile cycle that burns ATP and dumps it as heat with no net product. Regulation, not the energy cost, is what holds that in check.
scenes.notes: Why does gluconeogenesis need its own enzymes instead of just reversing glycolysis? Think of it as a bargain the cell strikes with thermodynamics. Glycolysis releases energy, about seventy-four kilojoules per mole, so it is downhill and spontaneous. Gluconeogenesis consumes energy, and that extra cost, the six nucleotide-triphosphate equivalents, is precisely what tips the synthetic direction to also be favorable. If synthesis were free, both pathways would run at once in the same cell, a futile cycle that burns ATP and dumps it as heat with no net product. The energy cost is not waste; it is the price of directional control.
